How does latency differ between RAG and.snippet: # Long context vs RAG for real apps: costs, latency, and accuracy. We examine both long context language models (also referred to as long context models) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows, which involve a two-step process of retrieving relevant information and generating responses. Long-context LLMs can handle context windows up to a million tokens, significantly larger than traditional models, enabling them to process extensive information in a single inference. There are two honest ways to give models more knowledge at inference time: make the context window bigger with long context models, or fetch the right text on demand using RAG workflows. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieves relevant external documents to augment the model’s input dynamically, while long-context LLMs rely on a very large fixed context window to process all information directly. It refers to the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single input prompt, including both user input and any additional context.

How does latency differ between RAG and.snippet: Long context approaches process every token through the model, while RAG selectively retrieves only relevant sections. For AI apps requiring interactive response times under 2 seconds, well-optimized RAG pipelines can often hit that target, while naive long-context prompting on very large inputs may struggle to do so. For retrieval-style queries where most context goes unused, RAG avoids paying for tokens the model doesn't need. Long context models tend to demonstrate superior performance for full-document understanding, while RAG often excels when factual accuracy, traceability, and cost constraints are primary concerns. Cost sensitivity matters most for retrieval-style queries, where RAG can operate at a fraction of long context costs. Route cost-sensitive queries through RAG while reserving long-context processing for tasks requiring full corpus analysis. Consider starting with RAG for cost-effective, fast retrieval over large knowledge bases—for retrieval-style queries, it can operate at a fraction of large context window costs.

What metrics can be used to evaluate ans.snippet: Because failures can originate in either the retrieval component or the generation component, the most useful RAG evaluation strategies test the retriever and generator independently before measuring end-to-end performance. This matters for RAG evaluation pipelines because it means you’re not locked into proprietary models for your judge — platforms like Opik let you swap in any LLM supported by LiteLLM, including open-source options, as your evaluation backbone. Context precision penalizes systems that rank relevant documents lower, while context recall measures whether the retriever surfaced all the relevant information the expected answer requires. ### What does answer relevance measure in RAG evaluation? from opik.evaluation import evaluate from opik.evaluation.metrics import ( Hallucination, ContextPrecision, ContextRecall, AnswerRelevance ) metrics = [ Hallucination(), ContextPrecision(), ContextRecall(), AnswerRelevance(), ] results = evaluate( dataset=your_dataset, task=your_rag_pipeline, scoring_metrics=metrics, experiment_config={ "model": "gpt-4o", "chunk_size": 512, "top_k": 5, }, ). Start with the RAG Triad: context relevance to verify your retriever, faithfulness to catch hallucinations, and answer relevance to ensure you’re actually helping users.
